**Proposition 3 (California General Election, November 3, 2026)**

**Official title:** "PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES." It is a citizen initiative to amend the state constitution, qualified through signature gathering.

**Summary**
- Applies to people earning more than $371,000, a threshold that rises yearly with inflation.
- Would make permanent the tax rates voters previously approved for those earners.
- Directs the revenue to public education. The title also mentions health care, but the summary does not.
- **Supporters:** California Teachers Association, CA School Nurses Organization, California State PTA, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
- **Opponents:** California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

**Yes vote:** The higher income tax on top earners, which dates to 2012, would stay in force permanently rather than end in 2031.

**No vote:** The higher income tax on top earners would end in 2031 and not be made permanent.

**Fiscal impact:** Would keep between $5 billion and $15 billion in yearly revenue from state income taxes that would otherwise stop when the time-limited increase ends in 2031.

**Arguments for (supporters)**
- Says it "prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires" by keeping rates the top 2% have been paying for a decade and a half.
- Argues it protects school and health care funding and doesn't raise voters' taxes.
- Says it adds accountability rules and audits so school money reaches classrooms.
- Urges a yes vote.

**Arguments against (opponents)**
- Argues residents already pay "the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes" and face the highest living costs.
- Says the measure turns a time-limited income tax permanent while state government throws away billions on programs that have failed, rather than what voters prioritize.
- Says the state should "Fix spending first" before the tax is made permanent.
- Urges a no vote.

**Election and other details**
- **Election Day:** November 3, 2026. Voting runs from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
- **Ballots:** Counties start sending them by October 5, 2026.
- **Registration deadline:** October 19, 2026.
- **Other formats:** The guide is available as PDFs in nine other languages, plus audio, large print, and American Sign Language versions.
- **Campaign contacts:** For: 555 Capitol Mall, Suite 400, Sacramento, CA 95814; YesProp3CA.com; info@YesProp3CA.com. Against: VoteNoProp3.com; info@VoteNoProp3.com.
- The page also links to a polling place finder and to separate pages for the analysis, arguments and rebuttals, and full text, which aren't included here.

content.content:
**Overview:** Prop. 3 would make permanent an income tax on high earners that California voters first approved in 2012 and renewed in 2016. The current tax expires in 2031, and voters decide the measure on Nov. 3.

**What it does**
- Applies to individuals earning over $371,000 a year and to couples earning over $743,000.
- Revenue has ranged from $5 billion to $15 billion a year, shifting with market performance, borrowing costs, and other factors that affect top earners' income.
- Top earners would keep a 12.3% rate. Adding the state's extra 1% levy on income above $1 million (which funds mental health services) brings the combined rate to 13.3%, the nation's highest.
- Most money would flow through Proposition 98, which sets 40% of the state budget aside for public schools and community colleges. The split is 89% K-12 and 11% community colleges. Revenue above a set threshold would go to a rainy-day reserve.
- The LAO says the measure also funds health care and other services by freeing up money that would otherwise go to schools.
- In strong revenue years, the tax accounts for about 15% of the state's total K-12 funding.

**Supporters**
- The California Teachers Association, led by David Goldberg, is the main backer. It gathered thousands of signatures to qualify the measure and had members canvass more than 200,000 doors statewide. Goldberg called the effort "one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet."
- Goldberg says: "It's only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it's vital for our schools." He warns that rejection would bring layoffs of as many as 50,000 teachers, along with other reductions.
- Children Now's Rob Manwaring also argues schools need more funding. He links high student-to-teacher ratios to a large achievement gap. NCES data shows one teacher per 22 students in 2022-23, versus a national average of 1:15. He also warns that federal cuts and a possible downturn could squeeze budgets.

**Opponents**
- Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, argues schools may not need more funding, citing recent state investments and falling enrollment. Enrollment has dropped by more than half a million students since the mid-2010s.
- She says some districts have unaffordable labor contracts: "It's not sustainable."
- She argues California already has the nation's steepest income tax rate and that higher taxes would push wealthy residents out, disproportionately hurting state revenue. LAO analysis finds the highest-earning 2% pay roughly half of state income taxes.

**Money**
- Supporters: The union and other groups have raised "more than $40 million" to pass Prop. 3.
- Opponents, including taxpayer groups, have raised $5,500.
- These are fundraising totals only. The article reports no spending figures and no dates for either total.

**Polling**
- A September PPIC survey found 58% of likely voters said they would vote yes.
- Democrats backed it at 82%, compared with 18% of Republicans.

**Predictions on passage**
- The article includes no analyst forecast of whether Prop. 3 will pass. The closest signal is the poll, and the article says the measure "appears to have an edge with voters."
- LAO analysis covers how the money would flow and how much top earners pay, not the vote.
- Goldberg's layoff warning describes what would happen if the measure fails, not the odds that it will.

**2012 and 2016 history**
- Voters first approved the tax in 2012 as a temporary measure meant to help schools weather the Great Recession.
- Voters extended it in 2016.
- This is the third time the tax has been on California ballots. The union put it on the ballot more than four years before expiration, since districts plan budgets well in advance.
- The article doesn't name the 2012 or 2016 measures as Prop. 30 or Prop. 55 and gives no vote totals, so I can't confirm those details from it.

**Related: Prop. 40**
- Prop. 40 would put a 5% levy on Californians with assets above $1 billion. It would send 90% of proceeds to health care and the rest to schools, nutrition aid, and other programs.
- The union opposes it, arguing schools would get too little. Goldberg said: "We're not campaigning against Prop. 40. We're just prioritizing Prop. 3."

**Proposition 3 summary**

**What it does**
- Removes the 2031 expiration from "existing voter-approved tax rates" for high earners.
- Voters approved the higher rates twice, in 2012 and 2016, each time as a temporary measure.
- The official title says the measure provides "permanent funding for schools and health care." The ballot language says it "Allocates tax revenues to public education."
- A "Yes" vote makes the increase permanent. A "No" vote lets the higher rate expire in 2031.

- Single filers earning "over $371,000," a threshold "adjusted annually for inflation."
- Joint filers earning "more than $743,000" a year.
- Current rate: "between 10.3% and 12.3%," varying by income level.
- If the measure fails, the rate would fall to "9.3%" in 2031.

- The rate ends in 2031. The opening line says "after 2030," but the rest of the page says "in 2031."

- The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) says the rates bring in "between $5 billion and $15 billion per year."
